title: Timers and counters
goals: Say what an on-delay (TON), off-delay (TOF) and pulse (TP) timer do, from IN to Q, and what ET shows
Write a preset time the IEC way (T#5s, T#500ms) and work out when Q comes on
Count parts with a counter (CTU, CTD) and a reset, and say when its Q comes on
Build a start-up warning (delay on) and a run-on (delay off) for a conveyor or fan
Say what happens to an on-delay when IN drops early, and when a retentive timer is needed
summary:
A timer is a **block**: you give it an input **IN** and a **preset time PT**; it gives an output **Q** and the **elapsed time ET**. Times are written `T#5s`, `T#500ms`, `T#1m30s`.

- **TON (on-delay):** Q comes on once IN has been on for PT **without a break**. ET counts up while IN is on. IN off: Q off and ET back to 0 at once. A short blip of IN does nothing.
- **TOF (off-delay):** Q comes on with IN at once, and **stays on for PT after IN goes off**. If IN comes back during that time, the timing starts again. A run-on.
- **TP (pulse):** a rising IN gives a pulse exactly PT long, however long IN lasts.

Allen-Bradley calls Q **.DN** (done) and ET **.ACC**. A timer is accurate to about one scan.

A **retentive** on-delay (Siemens TONR, Allen-Bradley RTO) keeps its ET when IN drops, and adds up the on-time until it is reset. Use it for run hours, not for a delay.

A counter counts **rising edges**, not scans: holding its input on counts once.

- **CTU (count up):** each rising edge of **CU** adds 1 to the count **CV**. Q comes on when CV reaches the preset **PV**. **R** sets CV back to 0.
- **CTD (count down):** **LD** loads CV with PV; each rising edge of **CD** takes 1 off. Q comes on when CV reaches 0.

Two patterns you will use every week:

- **Start-up warning:** a horn sounds for a few seconds before a conveyor moves: a TON on the start request; horn while not done, conveyor once done.
- **Run-on:** a fan keeps cooling after a drive stops: a TOF with the drive's run signal as IN.

formulas.name: When an on-delay is done
formulas.says: An on-delay's Q comes on PT after IN last came on and stayed on. Any earlier stretch of IN that broke off early does not count.
symbols: when IN came on for the last time before it stayed on
the preset time (one name, not P times T)
formulas.example: PT = 5 s, IN on at 2 s for good: Q on at $2 + 5 = 7$ s.

formulas.name: Counts to go
formulas.says: How many more rising edges an up-counter needs before its Q comes on.
formulas.example: PV = 24 bottles a crate, CV = 17: $24 - 17 = 7$ more.

bench.task: On a trainer or a spare PLC (24 V DC inputs), make a **start-up warning**: holding a selector switch on sounds a buzzer or lights a lamp for 5 s, then turns on a second output for the conveyor.
check: Watch ET count up online in the programming software while the selector is on
Switch off after 3 s and on again: the 5 s starts again from 0
Change PT to T#2s online (or download), and time it with a stopwatch
Add a counter that counts how many times the conveyor output came on, and a reset button

cards.q: Have a go: a guess is fine. An on-delay timer has PT = T#5s. Its input IN comes on for 3 s, goes off for 1 s, then comes on and stays on. When does its output Q come on, counting from the very start?
cards.why: An on-delay needs IN on for the whole 5 s **without a break**. The first 3 s are thrown away when IN goes off. IN comes back at 4 s, so Q comes on at $4 + 5 = 9$ s. Adding the 3 s to the next 2 s (to give 5 s at 6 s) is how a retentive timer would behave, not an ordinary one.

cards.title: A timer is a block
cards.body:
A timer is a **block** you call each scan. You give it:

- **IN**: what starts it timing
- **PT**: the preset time, written `T#5s`, `T#500ms`, `T#1m30s`

It gives back:

- **Q**: its output, a bit
- **ET**: the elapsed time so far

In Structured Text: `T1(IN := Start_Req, PT := T#5s);` then `T1.Q` is its output. Each timer is its own **instance**, T1, T2 and so on, with its own memory.

Allen-Bradley names them differently: the preset is **.PRE**, the elapsed time **.ACC**, and Q is **.DN**, done.
cards.more:
Think of a kitchen timer with a button you must keep pressed. IN is your finger on the button; PT is the time set on the dial; ET is how far round it has got; Q is the bell.

`T#` means "a time". T#5s is 5 seconds; T#500ms is half a second; T#1m30s is ninety seconds. Writing `5` alone would not do: the PLC would not know whether you meant seconds or milliseconds.

You can have as many timers as you like, each with its own name. T1 timing does not affect T2.

cards.q: Which is the IEC way to write a preset of one and a half seconds?
cards.why: `T#` marks a time and the unit is written with it: T#1500ms (or T#1s500ms, or T#1.5s). A bare 1.5 or 1500 is just a number, with no unit, and T#1.5 has no unit either.

cards.title: TON: the on-delay
cards.body:
An **on-delay** makes Q wait. Once IN has been on for PT **without a break**, Q comes on.

- While IN is on, ET counts up from 0, and stops at PT.
- When IN goes off, Q goes off and ET goes back to **0** at once.

So a short blip of IN does nothing: it has to last the whole PT. That makes a TON good for **filtering** a jittery signal (a level switch in a sloshing tank), and for **delays** (wait 5 s before starting).

In the picture, Go drives a TON with PT = T#3s. Switch Go on and watch ET.
cards.more:
Draw it as a timeline, with time along the bottom.

IN goes on at 2 s. ET starts counting: 0 at 2 s, 1 s at 3 s, 2 s at 4 s, 3 s at 5 s. At 5 s ET reaches PT = 3 s and Q comes on. Q stays on for as long as IN does.

Now suppose IN had gone off at 4 s instead. ET was at 2 s; it drops straight back to 0 and Q never came on. When IN comes back, the count starts again from 0.

The rule: **Q on = IN has been on for at least PT, continuously**.

cards.intro: Go drives an on-delay, PT = T#3s. The lamp is its Q.

predict.q: You will switch Go on, then off again after about **2 seconds**, before the 3 s are up. What will the lamp do?
predict.why: IN did not stay on for the whole PT, so Q never came on, and ET went back to 0 when Go went off.

ask.q: Now leave Go on until the lamp lights, then switch Go off. What happens to the lamp and to ET?
options: The lamp goes out at once and ET goes back to 0
The lamp stays on for another 3 s
The lamp stays on until you press Reset
ET stays at 3 s and the lamp stays on
ask.why: An on-delay only delays switching **on**. Switching off is immediate: IN off means Q off and ET = 0. Delaying the switch-off is a different timer, the TOF.

cards.title: TOF and TP: off-delay and pulse
cards.body:
**TOF, the off-delay.** Q comes on **with** IN, at once. When IN goes off, Q **stays on for PT**, then goes off. If IN comes back meanwhile, the timing starts again. Use it for a **run-on**: a cooling fan that keeps going for two minutes after the drive stops.

**TP, the pulse.** When IN rises, Q gives one pulse exactly PT long, whether IN is let go early or held on longer. Use it for a fixed-length shot: a lubrication squirt, a 2 s horn.

TON delays the start; TOF delays the stop; TP makes a pulse of fixed length.
cards.more:
The same timeline for each, with PT = 3 s and IN on from 2 s to 4 s:

- **TON**: IN was on for only 2 s, less than PT. Q never comes on.
- **TOF**: Q comes on at 2 s with IN. IN goes off at 4 s; Q stays on 3 s more, until 7 s.
- **TP**: Q comes on at 2 s and goes off at 5 s, exactly 3 s later, even though IN went off at 4 s.

A stairwell light on a timer is a TP: press the button, get a fixed time of light. A fan that runs on after you switch off the bathroom light is a TOF.

cards.q: A drive's cooling fan must keep running for 2 minutes after the drive stops, and run all the time the drive runs. The drive's running signal is Drive_Run. Which timer, with which input?
options: A TOF with IN := Drive_Run, PT := T#2m
A TON with IN := Drive_Run, PT := T#2m
A TP with IN := Drive_Run, PT := T#2m
A TON with IN := NOT Drive_Run, PT := T#2m
cards.why: The fan must come on at once and go off late: that is an off-delay. A TON would start the fan 2 minutes **after** the drive started, which is backwards. A TP would give 2 minutes from the start, whatever the drive did.

cards.title: Counters count edges
cards.body:
An **up-counter, CTU**, adds 1 to its count **CV** each time its input **CU** goes from 0 to 1: a **rising edge**. Holding CU on counts once, not once a scan.

When CV reaches the preset **PV**, Q comes on. **R** (reset) puts CV back to 0.

A **down-counter, CTD**, works the other way: **LD** (load) sets CV to PV, each rising edge of **CD** takes 1 off, and Q comes on at 0. Use it to count down what is left: 24 bottles still to go in the crate.

In the picture, press Part three times.
cards.more:
Why edges? A box takes maybe half a second to pass a photo-eye. With a 5 ms scan that is about 100 scans with the input on. Counting scans would count one box as 100.

So the counter remembers what CU was last scan, and counts only when it was 0 and is now 1: the moment the box arrives.

A crate holds 24 bottles: PV = 24. Each bottle passing the sensor adds 1. At CV = 24, Q comes on: swap the crate. A reset button, or the crate-changed signal, puts CV back to 0 for the next one.

cards.intro: An up-counter with PV = 3. Part and Reset are push-buttons.

predict.q: If you press Part once and **hold it down** for several seconds, what will CV show?
predict.why: A counter counts the rising edge, the moment the input goes from 0 to 1. Holding it on is still one edge.

ask.q: Press Part until Full comes on, then twice more. What is CV, and is Full on?
options: CV = 5 and Full is on: the count carries on past PV, and Q is on while CV ≥ PV
CV = 3 and Full is on: it stops at PV
CV = 0 and Full is off: it wraps round
ask.why: An IEC CTU keeps counting past PV (up to the limit of its number type), and Q means CV ≥ PV. Only R brings it back to 0. That is why a counter usually wants a reset once its batch is done.

cards.q: A conveyor must sound a horn for 5 s before it moves, every time it is started. The operator holds a Run switch on to run it. Write it in Structured Text with one TON.

steps.show: The Run switch: `T1(IN := Run, PT := T#5s);`. The 5 s start when Run goes on.
While Run is on and the timer is not yet done: `Horn := Run AND NOT T1.Q;`
Once the timer is done: `Conveyor := T1.Q;`. T1.Q is only on while Run is on, so switching Run off stops it at once.

steps.ask: Check: Run is switched off after 3 s and on again.
steps.show: IN went off, so ET went back to 0: the horn sounds for a full 5 s again. Good: a warning is never cut short.

cards.why: One on-delay gives both: before it is done is the warning, after it is done is the run. Using `NOT T1.Q` for the horn means the two can never be on together.

cards.context: The start-up warning: `T1(IN := Run, PT := T#5s); Horn := Run AND NOT T1.Q; Conveyor := T1.Q;`
cards.q: Why is Horn `Run AND NOT T1.Q`, and not just `NOT T1.Q`?
cards.model: `NOT T1.Q` alone is 1 whenever the timer is not done, and that includes all the time the conveyor is switched off: the horn would sound day and night. ANDing it with Run limits it to the time between switching Run on and the timer finishing, which is exactly the warning period. As soon as T1.Q comes on, `NOT T1.Q` goes to 0 and the horn stops as the conveyor starts.
points: NOT T1.Q is also true while the conveyor is off
Run limits the horn to after the switch is turned on
The horn stops at the moment T1.Q starts the conveyor

cards.q: A drive's cooling fan must run whenever the drive runs, and for 90 s after it stops. The drive's running signal is Drive_Run. Write it with one timer.

steps.show: An off-delay: `T2(IN := Drive_Run, PT := T#90s);` (or T#1m30s).
`Fan := T2.Q;`: on with the drive, and for 90 s after.

steps.ask: The drive restarts 30 s after stopping. What does the fan do?
steps.show: It never went off; IN is back on, so the off-delay starts again from 0 next time the drive stops.

cards.why: An off-delay's Q follows IN on at once and lets go late. Restarting inside the delay just cancels the run-on.

cards.q: An on-delay has PT = T#{p}s. Its IN comes on at 0 s for {a} s, goes off for {g} s, then comes on and stays on. When does Q come on, in seconds from the start?
cards.hint: Does the first {a} s count towards the on-delay once IN has gone off?
cards.work: The first {a} s are lost when IN goes off. IN comes back at {a} + {g} s, and Q comes on PT = {p} s after that: $t_Q = t_{on} + PT = {answer}$ s.
cards.why: An ordinary on-delay resets whenever IN goes off, so only the last unbroken stretch counts. Adding the first stretch to the second is what a retentive timer does.

cards.q: Count bottles into a crate of 24. Crate_Full comes on at 24; Crate_Changed resets the count. Fill in the blanks.

tests.name: Full at 24, and a held sensor counts once

cards.why: PV is the count at which Q comes on; R puts CV back to 0. The sensor held on for ten scans still counted once: a counter counts rising edges.

cards.q: An on-delay has PT = T#{p}s. Its IN has been on for {a} s. What does its ET show, in milliseconds?
cards.work: IN has been on {a} s, less than PT, so ET is still counting: {a} s = {answer} ms.
cards.why: ET counts up while IN is on and stops at PT. {a} s is under {p} s, so ET is simply the time IN has been on. (ET = PT only once Q is on.)

cards.q: A down-counter is loaded with PV = {pv} labels on a new reel. {n} labels have been used. What is CV?
cards.work: LD set CV to {pv}; each label took one off: {pv} − {n} = {answer}.
cards.why: A CTD counts down from PV. Its Q comes on at 0: time to change the reel.

cards.q: An up-counter packs {pv} boxes to a pallet. Its CV reads {cv}. How many more boxes before its Q comes on?
cards.why: Q comes on when CV reaches PV, so the boxes still to come are the difference.

cards.q: Why does a counter count rising edges rather than counting every scan its input is on?
options: A part stays in front of a sensor for many scans; counting scans would count one part many times
Rising edges are faster to read
So that it can count backwards
cards.why: At a few milliseconds a scan, a box half a second in front of a photo-eye is on for about a hundred scans. The edge is the one moment each box arrives.

cards.q: A cooling fan should run with the drive and for 60 s after it stops. Instead the fan only starts 60 s after the drive starts. Which line is wrong?
cards.fix: `VAR T3 : TOF; END_VAR`: an off-delay, not an on-delay.
cards.why: The call and the output are fine. The timer is the wrong kind: a TON delays switching on, which is exactly the fault seen. A run-on is an off-delay.

cards.q: Match each job to the timer for it.
pairs: A 3 s horn before a press closes
TON: Q waits PT after IN comes on
A fan that runs on for 2 minutes after the drive stops
TOF: Q stays on PT after IN goes off
Exactly 0.5 s of grease each time a button is pressed
TP: one pulse PT long from each rising IN
Hours run by a pump, kept across stops, for its service interval
A retentive on-delay (TONR, RTO), reset at service
cards.why: Delay the start: TON. Delay the stop: TOF. A fixed pulse: TP. Add up time across many runs: retentive, because an ordinary TON forgets the moment IN goes off.

cards.q: A counter on a photo-eye sometimes counts one box twice. The box is shiny and the beam flickers as it passes. What is the best fix?
options: Bridge the flicker: a short off-delay (a few tens of ms) on the sensor signal before the counter
A short on-delay on the sensor signal before the counter
Count every scan instead of edges
cards.why: The flicker is a brief drop in the middle of the box, and its return is a second rising edge, which the counter rightly counts. An off-delay keeps its Q on through a gap shorter than PT, so the counter sees one pulse per box. An on-delay does not help: it drops out the moment the input drops, then gives a second edge when it comes back. Many sensors have an off-delay setting built in for exactly this. Changing PV only hides the fault.

cards.q: A motor is started by a Start push-button with a seal-in, and should stop by itself 10 minutes later. Which is right?
options: A TON with IN := Motor, PT := T#10m, and NOT T1.Q in series in the motor's seal-in rung
A TOF with IN := Start, PT := T#10m, driving the motor
A counter counting scans up to 10 minutes
cards.why: The motor's own bit times how long it has run; when T1.Q comes on, the NOT T1.Q contact breaks the seal-in and the motor stops. A TP started by the motor would also give 10 minutes, but it would not reset if the motor was stopped and restarted early. Counting scans makes the time depend on the scan time.

cards.q: An on-delay has PT = T#4s. IN comes on for 2 s, goes off for 1 s, then stays on. When does Q come on, from the start?
cards.why: The first 2 s are lost when IN goes off. IN comes back at 3 s, and Q comes on 4 s after that: 7 s.

cards.q: An off-delay has PT = T#5s. IN goes on at 0 s and off at 2 s. When is Q on?
cards.why: A TOF's Q follows IN on at once, at 0 s, and stays on for PT after IN goes off: 2 + 5 = 7 s.

cards.q: A pump must run for exactly 20 s each time a Fill push-button is pressed, however briefly it is pressed. Choose the timer.

tests.name: A short press gives the full 20 s
Holding it longer still gives 20 s

cards.why: A pulse timer turns a rising edge into a pulse exactly PT long. A TON would not start until Fill had been held 20 s; a TOF would run 20 s after the button was released, plus however long it was held.
